cards.cue: 'Instances in a private subnet must reach S3 without traversing a NAT gateway; the solution must add no cost.'
cards.answer: VPC gateway endpoint for S3
cards.why: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, are free, and are added as route-table entries. Interface endpoints cost per hour and per GB; NAT gateway charges per GB processed.
distractors: NAT instance in the public subnet

cards.cue: SG vs NACL: which one is stateless and therefore needs an explicit rule for ephemeral ports 1024-65535?
cards.answer: Network ACL
cards.why: NACLs evaluate each packet independently with numbered allow/deny rules; return traffic must be allowed explicitly. Security groups are stateful and only have allow rules.
distractors: Neither - the VPC router handles return traffic

cards.cue: 'Block a single malicious public IP from reaching any instance in a subnet.'
cards.answer: Add a DENY rule for that IP in the subnet's network ACL
cards.why: Security groups cannot deny; NACLs can. A low-numbered deny rule blocks before the allow rules are evaluated.
distractors: Add a deny rule in the security group
Attach a WAF web ACL to the subnet
Remove the route to the internet gateway

cards.cue: Spot the trap: 'An IAM user has AdministratorAccess in a member account but receives AccessDenied when launching EC2 in eu-west-1. Fix: attach another admin policy.'
cards.answer: Wrong - an SCP (or permission boundary / explicit deny) is capping the account; identity policies cannot override a ceiling
cards.why: SCPs bound every principal in member accounts including root; more identity permissions change nothing. Check the OU's SCP for a Region deny.
distractors: Wrong - the user must use the management account

cards.cue: Which policy type caps the maximum permissions of ONE IAM role inside an account (e.g., developers may create roles but only within limits)?
cards.answer: IAM permission boundary
cards.why: A boundary is a managed policy attached to a user/role that sets its ceiling; combine with an iam:PermissionsBoundary condition on iam:CreateRole. SCPs work at the account/OU level.

cards.cue: 'Account B's Lambda needs to read objects in Account A's bucket; the Lambda must keep its own identity and access its own account's resources in the same call.'
cards.answer: Bucket policy in Account A granting Account B's role + identity policy in Account B allowing s3:GetObject
cards.why: A resource-based policy grants cross-account access without switching identity. AssumeRole would swap to Account A's identity and lose access to Account B resources for that call.
distractors: Create an IAM user in Account A and share keys
Have the Lambda assume a role in Account A
Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication into Account B

cards.cue: 'Employees authenticate with the corporate SAML 2.0 identity provider and need CLI/console access to 40 AWS accounts with role-based permission sets.'
cards.answer: AWS IAM Identity Center
cards.why: Identity Center gives workforce SSO across Organizations accounts with permission sets and SAML/SCIM to the IdP. Cognito is for application end users; IAM users would mean 40 sets of credentials.

cards.cue: Cognito user pool vs identity pool: which one issues temporary AWS credentials so a mobile app can upload directly to S3 (including unauthenticated guests)?
cards.answer: Cognito identity pool (federated identities)
cards.why: Identity pools exchange an identity token (from a user pool, Google, SAML, or guest) for STS credentials. User pools handle sign-up/sign-in and issue JWTs for API Gateway.

cards.cue: STS AssumeRole session duration: minimum, maximum, and cap when role chaining?
cards.answer: 15 minutes to 12 hours; role chaining max 1 hour
cards.why: MaxSessionDuration is set on the role (default 1 h). Chained AssumeRole calls are hard-capped at 1 h regardless.

cards.cue: 'Existing RDS MySQL instance is unencrypted; compliance now requires encryption at rest.' Tempting: modify the instance and tick 'enable encryption'.
cards.answer: Take a snapshot, copy it with a KMS key, restore a new encrypted instance and repoint the app
cards.why: Encryption can only be set at creation. The copy-snapshot-with-encryption path is the only route for RDS and EBS. Replicas inherit the primary's state.
distractors: Modify the instance and enable encryption
Create an encrypted read replica and promote it
Enable SSE-KMS on the RDS storage bucket

cards.cue: 'Every use of the key that encrypts S3 objects must be logged and auditors must see who decrypted what.' Which S3 encryption mode?
cards.answer: SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key
cards.why: Only KMS-backed encryption produces CloudTrail entries per key use and lets you control the key policy. SSE-S3 has no per-key audit; SSE-C means you manage keys yourself.
distractors: Client-side encryption with S3 default keys

cards.cue: Which KMS key types support automatic rotation, and what rotation period can you set on a customer-managed key?
cards.answer: AWS-managed keys (fixed yearly) and customer-managed SYMMETRIC keys with KMS-generated material (optional; period configurable 90-2,560 days, default 365, plus on-demand rotation)
cards.why: Imported key material and asymmetric/HMAC keys cannot auto-rotate; rotate them manually by creating a new key and moving the alias. AWS-managed key rotation cannot be changed.
distractors: All customer-managed keys including asymmetric, any period
Only keys with imported key material, yearly

cards.cue: KMS: scheduled key deletion waiting period range, and max plaintext size for a direct Encrypt call?
cards.answer: 7-30 days; 4 KB
cards.why: Deletion is irreversible so KMS forces a 7-30 day pending window. Anything over 4 KB uses envelope encryption via GenerateDataKey.

cards.cue: 'Regulation requires single-tenant FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated hardware where AWS operators can never access key material; Oracle TDE must use it.'
cards.answer: AWS CloudHSM (hsm2m.medium is FIPS 140-3 L3; hsm1.medium FIPS 140-2 L3)
cards.why: CloudHSM is single-tenant hardware where only you hold the keys; supports PKCS#11/JCE, Oracle TDE, SSL offload, and can back a KMS custom key store. KMS HSMs are also FIPS 140-3 L3 validated but multi-tenant and AWS-operated - the discriminator is exclusive key custody, not the FIPS level.
distractors: AWS KMS with imported key material

cards.cue: 'Rotate the Aurora master password every 30 days automatically with the least operational overhead.'
cards.answer: AWS Secrets Manager with managed rotation
cards.why: Secrets Manager has native rotation for RDS/Aurora/Redshift/DocumentDB. Parameter Store SecureString stores secrets but has no built-in rotation.
distractors: IAM database authentication tokens stored in DynamoDB

cards.cue: Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store: which is free for standard parameters up to 4 KB but does not rotate?
cards.answer: SSM Parameter Store
cards.why: Standard tier is free (10,000 params, 4 KB); advanced tier costs $0.05/param with 8 KB and policies. Secrets Manager is $0.40/secret/month and rotates.

cards.cue: 'Public TLS certificate for an ALB and a CloudFront distribution; certificates must renew automatically at no cost.' Where must the CloudFront certificate live?
cards.answer: AWS Certificate Manager, with the CloudFront certificate requested in us-east-1
cards.why: ACM public certs are free and auto-renew but only attach to integrated services (ELB, CloudFront, API Gateway). CloudFront reads certificates from us-east-1 only; ACM certs cannot be exported to EC2.
distractors: ACM in the ALB's Region for both
Import a Let's Encrypt cert into IAM
ACM Private CA in any Region

cards.cue: 'Administrators need shell access to EC2 in private subnets; security forbids inbound ports, SSH keys, and bastion hosts; sessions must be logged.'
cards.answer: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager
cards.why: Session Manager uses the SSM agent's outbound channel, IAM for authorization, and logs to S3/CloudWatch. A bastion still opens port 22 and needs key management.
distractors: Bastion host in a public subnet

cards.cue: 'A web app on EC2 has an SSRF flaw; attackers could read the instance role credentials from the metadata service.' Fix?
cards.answer: Require IMDSv2 (HttpTokens = required) in the launch template
cards.why: IMDSv2 needs a PUT to obtain a session token with a hop limit; SSRF via GET cannot complete it. Removing the role or rotating keys does not close the hole.
distractors: Remove the instance profile and use access keys

cards.cue: 'Block SQL injection and cross-site scripting and rate-limit abusive IPs on an application served by an ALB.'
cards.answer: AWS WAF web ACL on the ALB
cards.why: WAF inspects L7 HTTP requests with managed rule groups and rate-based rules; attaches to ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, AppSync (not NLB). Shield handles volumetric DDoS, not request content.

cards.cue: Shield Standard vs Shield Advanced: which is free and automatic, and what does Advanced cost with commitment?
cards.answer: Standard is free for everyone (L3/L4); Advanced is $3,000/month with a 1-year commitment (L7 protection, SRT, cost protection)
cards.why: Advanced adds application-layer DDoS mitigation, 24x7 Shield Response Team, and refunds for scaling charges on EC2/ELB/CloudFront/GA/Route 53.
distractors: Standard free; Advanced $30,000/yr with no commitment

cards.cue: Which service does WHAT: 'detect compromised credentials and crypto-mining from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs with one click'?
cards.answer: Amazon GuardDuty
cards.why: GuardDuty is agentless threat detection over account logs. Inspector scans for CVEs, Macie finds PII in S3, Detective investigates findings.

cards.cue: 'Continuously scan EC2 instances, ECR container images and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and unintended network exposure.'
cards.answer: Amazon Inspector
cards.why: Inspector is the vulnerability scanner (via SSM agent for EC2). GuardDuty looks for threats in logs; Security Hub only aggregates.

cards.cue: 'Identify S3 buckets that contain personally identifiable information and alert on public exposure.'
cards.answer: Amazon Macie
cards.why: Macie uses ML to classify sensitive data in S3 and reports bucket exposure. Access Analyzer finds external-access policies but not data content.

cards.cue: Config vs CloudTrail vs CloudWatch: which answers 'who deleted the security group rule and when'?
cards.answer: AWS CloudTrail
cards.why: CloudTrail records API calls with caller identity (90-day event history, trails to S3 for longer). Config shows the configuration timeline and compliance; CloudWatch is metrics/logs.

cards.cue: 'Detect any security group that allows 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 across all accounts and automatically remediate.'
cards.answer: AWS Config rule (restricted-ssh) with SSM Automation remediation, aggregated across the organization
cards.why: Config evaluates resource configuration against rules and can trigger remediation. CloudTrail only logs the API call; GuardDuty detects threats, not misconfigurations per se.

cards.cue: 'Find every IAM role, S3 bucket, and KMS key that is shared with principals outside the organization.'
cards.answer: IAM Access Analyzer
cards.why: Access Analyzer reasons over resource policies against a zone of trust (account or org) and reports external access; also validates policies and generates least-privilege policies from CloudTrail.

cards.cue: 'Centrally enforce WAF rules and security-group baselines on all current AND future accounts in the organization.'
cards.answer: AWS Firewall Manager
cards.why: Firewall Manager pushes WAF, Shield Advanced, SG, Network Firewall and DNS Firewall policies org-wide and auto-covers new resources. Security Hub only reports.

cards.cue: 'Inspect all traffic between VPCs and to the internet with intrusion prevention (Suricata) rules and domain-name filtering, centrally.'
cards.answer: AWS Network Firewall (centralized via Transit Gateway inspection VPC)
cards.why: Network Firewall is the managed stateful L3-L7 firewall with IPS signatures. WAF only sees HTTP on supported services; NACLs are IP/port only; GWLB is for third-party appliances.
distractors: Gateway Load Balancer with no appliance

cards.cue: 'Objects must be retained 7 years and no one, not even the root user, may delete them before then.' Which Object Lock mode?
cards.answer: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode (versioning required)
cards.why: Compliance mode blocks everyone until retention expires. Governance mode lets users with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention override. Legal hold is indefinite and separate.
distractors: Glacier Vault Lock on a Standard bucket

cards.cue: S3 pre-signed URL maximum expiry when generated with IAM user credentials (SigV4)?
cards.answer: 7 days
cards.why: SigV4 pre-signed URLs cap at 7 days; role-based temporary credentials expire with the session (max 12 h). Console-generated defaults to shorter.

cards.cue: 'S3 bucket must be reachable only from the company's VPC and only over TLS.' Which bucket-policy conditions?
cards.answer: Deny unless aws:sourceVpce equals the endpoint ID; Deny when aws:SecureTransport is false
cards.why: aws:sourceVpce pins access to a gateway/interface endpoint; aws:SecureTransport=false denies HTTP. aws:SourceIp with private IPs does not work through endpoints.

cards.cue: 'Restrict an S3 origin so users can fetch content only through CloudFront, with SSE-KMS encrypted objects.'
cards.answer: CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) + bucket policy allowing the distribution
cards.why: OAC replaces OAI, signs requests with SigV4, and supports SSE-KMS and all Regions. Making the bucket public or using signed URLs alone does not block direct S3 access.
distractors: Public bucket with Referer header check

cards.cue: Interface endpoint vs gateway endpoint: which one can on-prem clients over Direct Connect use to reach S3 privately?
cards.answer: Interface endpoint (PrivateLink) for S3
cards.why: Gateway endpoints are route-table constructs usable only from inside the VPC; interface endpoints have ENIs with private IPs reachable via DX/VPN and peering.
distractors: Neither; on-prem must use the public S3 endpoint

cards.cue: 'Private connection from data center to AWS must be both consistent-bandwidth AND encrypted.' Tempting: Direct Connect alone.
cards.answer: Direct Connect with an IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over it (or MACsec on 10/100 Gbps dedicated ports)
cards.why: Direct Connect is private but not encrypted by default. Layer a VPN on the public VIF (or MACsec) to satisfy encryption.

cards.cue: VPC CIDR size limits and how many IPs AWS reserves per subnet?
cards.answer: /16 to /28; 5 reserved (network, router, DNS, future use, broadcast)
cards.why: A /28 has 16 addresses, 11 usable. Elastic IP default quota is also 5 per Region.

cards.cue: 'Troubleshoot why traffic from one instance to another is rejected; need accepted/rejected connection metadata without packet payloads.'
cards.answer: VPC Flow Logs (ENI, subnet or VPC level) to CloudWatch Logs or S3
cards.why: Flow Logs record 5-tuple + ACCEPT/REJECT. Traffic Mirroring captures full packets; CloudTrail is API calls; GuardDuty is threat detection.

cards.cue: 'Download the latest SOC 2 and PCI DSS reports for AWS services to give to auditors.'
cards.answer: AWS Artifact
cards.why: Artifact is the self-service portal for AWS compliance reports and agreements (BAA). Audit Manager collects your own evidence; Trusted Advisor is best-practice checks.

cards.cue: 'Set up a multi-account environment with preventive and detective guardrails and an automated account factory.'
cards.answer: AWS Control Tower
cards.why: Control Tower builds the landing zone on Organizations, applies SCP (preventive) and Config (detective) guardrails, and provisions accounts. Organizations alone lacks the guardrail automation.

cards.cue: 'A SaaS provider must expose an API to hundreds of customer VPCs; several customers use the same 10.0.0.0/16 CIDR; customers must not reach anything else.'
cards.answer: AWS PrivateLink: NLB-backed endpoint service; customers create interface endpoints
cards.why: PrivateLink is one-directional, ignores CIDR overlap and exposes only the service. Peering and TGW fail on overlapping CIDRs and expose the whole network.

cards.cue: 'Patch 500 EC2 instances and 200 on-prem servers on a maintenance schedule with compliance reporting.'
cards.answer: AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager (with Maintenance Windows, hybrid activations)
cards.why: Patch Manager applies baselines to EC2 and hybrid nodes via the SSM agent. Inspector finds CVEs but does not patch; Config reports drift.

cards.cue: 'Route on-prem DNS queries for internal.company.com to on-prem servers, and let on-prem resolve names in the VPC's private hosted zone.'
cards.answer: Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint + forwarding rules, and an inbound endpoint
cards.why: Outbound endpoints forward VPC queries to on-prem DNS; inbound endpoints accept queries from on-prem. Public hosted zones do not solve hybrid private names.
distractors: Public hosted zone with private records
DHCP option set pointing to on-prem DNS only
Route 53 private hosted zone shared via RAM

cards.cue: 'Database must survive an AZ failure with automatic failover and no application-side changes.' Tempting: cross-Region read replica.
cards.answer: RDS Multi-AZ deployment
cards.why: Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby and flips DNS automatically. Read replicas are async and require manual promotion, so they are not HA.

cards.cue: 'Reporting queries are slowing the production PostgreSQL RDS instance.' Tempting: enable Multi-AZ.
cards.answer: Create a read replica and point reporting at its endpoint
cards.why: Multi-AZ standby (instance deployment) is not readable. Read replicas offload reads asynchronously. (Multi-AZ DB cluster also gives readable standbys.)
distractors: Add ElastiCache in front of reports

cards.cue: RDS Multi-AZ instance vs Multi-AZ DB cluster: which has readable standbys and failover under 35 seconds?
cards.answer: Multi-AZ DB cluster (1 writer + 2 readable standbys, MySQL/PostgreSQL)
cards.why: The cluster deployment uses semi-synchronous replication to two readers with a reader endpoint. The instance deployment has one non-readable standby and 60-120 s failover.

cards.cue: Aurora storage: how many copies across how many AZs, and max read replicas?
cards.answer: 6 copies across 3 AZs; up to 15 replicas
cards.why: Writes need 4 of 6, reads 3 of 6; replicas are also failover targets by priority tier. RDS MySQL/PostgreSQL also allow 15 replicas but they are not automatic failover targets.

cards.cue: 'Relational database must fail over to a second Region within one minute with under a second of data loss.'
cards.answer: Aurora Global Database
cards.why: Storage-level replication gives <1 s lag, RPO ~1 s and RTO <1 min; managed failover offers RPO 0 for planned events. RDS cross-Region replicas lag minutes and need manual promotion.

cards.cue: Max automated backup retention for RDS/Aurora, and the DynamoDB point-in-time recovery window?
cards.answer: 35 days for both
cards.why: Longer retention requires manual snapshots or AWS Backup plans. Aurora Backtrack (MySQL) is separate: rewind up to 72 hours in place.

cards.cue: 'Recover an Aurora MySQL cluster to 10 minutes before a bad UPDATE without restoring to a new cluster or changing endpoints.'
cards.answer: Aurora Backtrack (up to 72 hours)
cards.why: Backtrack rewinds the existing cluster in place. PITR restores to a new cluster; snapshots need a restore; cloning creates a copy.

cards.cue: 'Active-active multi-Region key-value store; users read and write in their nearest Region.'
cards.answer: DynamoDB global tables
cards.why: Global tables replicate multi-master with ~1 s propagation (last writer wins). Aurora Global secondaries are read-only (write forwarding aside).

cards.cue: 'A three-tier app with one NAT gateway is unavailable when that NAT gateway's AZ fails.' Fix?
cards.answer: Deploy one NAT gateway per AZ and route each private subnet to its own AZ's NAT gateway
cards.why: NAT gateways are AZ-resident. A single one is a cross-AZ single point of failure and adds inter-AZ transfer charges.
distractors: Replace with a larger NAT gateway
Use a NAT instance with an Elastic IP
Enable Multi-AZ on the NAT gateway

cards.cue: Spot the trap: 'Instances behind the ALB return 502s but the ASG never replaces them, because they pass EC2 status checks.'
cards.answer: Switch the ASG health check type to ELB so app-level failures trigger replacement
cards.why: Default ASG health checks are EC2 status only. ELB health checks let the load balancer's target health mark instances unhealthy. Grace period must cover boot.
distractors: Increase the health check grace period
Set the termination policy to OldestInstance

cards.cue: ASG default cooldown, default health check grace period, and ELB default deregistration delay?
cards.answer: 300 seconds for all three
cards.why: Cooldown applies to simple scaling; grace period suppresses health checks after launch; deregistration delay drains connections before target removal.

cards.cue: Spot 2-minute warning: 'A stateful message broker runs on Spot to cut cost; it loses messages when interrupted.' Correct move?
cards.answer: Move the broker to On-Demand/Reserved or a managed service (Amazon MQ); keep Spot for stateless workers only
cards.why: Spot reclaims capacity with a 2-minute notice; stateful services cannot checkpoint fast enough. Capacity rebalancing helps stateless fleets, not brokers.
distractors: Add a second Spot instance in another AZ

cards.cue: 'Primary site is an ALB; if it fails, users must see a static maintenance page hosted in S3.' Which Route 53 setup?
cards.answer: Failover routing: primary alias to ALB with health check, secondary alias to the S3 static website
cards.why: Failover checks the primary's health and serves the secondary when unhealthy. Weighted or latency routing would send traffic to both.

cards.cue: 'Route 53 health checks show a private ALB as unhealthy even though it works.' Why, and fix?
cards.answer: Route 53 health checkers are on the public internet; use a CloudWatch alarm-based health check for private resources
cards.why: Endpoint health checks cannot reach private IPs. Calculated health checks only combine other checks.
distractors: Add the health checker IPs to the NACL allow list

cards.cue: 'RPO of minutes, RTO of tens of minutes, minimal ongoing cost: database replicated to DR Region, app servers off until needed.' Which DR strategy?
cards.answer: Pilot light
cards.why: Pilot light keeps only the data layer live (replica) with compute as AMIs/ASG at 0. Warm standby runs a scaled-down full stack (RTO minutes); backup/restore is hours.

cards.cue: DR ladder ordered by cost ascending: list the four strategies and their approximate RTO.
cards.answer: Backup & restore (hours) -> Pilot light (tens of minutes) -> Warm standby (minutes) -> Multi-site active/active (near zero)
cards.why: Cost rises and RTO/RPO fall along the ladder. Pick the leftmost rung that meets the stated RPO/RTO.
distractors: Backup -> Warm standby -> Pilot light -> Multi-site
Warm standby -> Pilot light -> Backup -> Multi-site

cards.cue: 'Continuous block-level replication of 300 on-prem servers to AWS so they can be launched in minutes after a disaster, paying only for storage until then.'
cards.answer: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
cards.why: DRS replicates to a low-cost staging area and launches recovery instances on demand (RPO seconds, RTO minutes). MGN is for one-way migration cutover; Backup is snapshot-based.

cards.cue: 'Centrally define backup schedules and retention for EBS, RDS, DynamoDB and EFS across 30 accounts, copy to another Region, and make backups immutable.'
cards.answer: AWS Backup with Organizations backup policies, cross-Region copy and Backup Vault Lock
cards.why: AWS Backup is the single policy-driven service across those resources. Data Lifecycle Manager covers EBS/AMIs only; scripts add overhead.

cards.cue: 'Bucket in us-east-1 must have an up-to-date copy in eu-west-1 for compliance, including objects already stored.' Prerequisite and extra step?
cards.answer: Enable versioning on both buckets, configure Cross-Region Replication, and run S3 Batch Replication for existing objects
cards.why: CRR requires versioning and replicates only new objects by default; Batch Replication backfills. RTC adds a 15-minute SLA if needed.
distractors: Enable CRR only - existing objects replicate automatically
Set a lifecycle rule to move objects to eu-west-1

cards.cue: S3 Replication Time Control SLA and S3 durability?
cards.answer: 99.99% of objects replicated within 15 minutes; 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability
cards.why: RTC is an add-on for replication with SLA-backed timing. All S3 classes share 11-nines durability; availability differs (99.99 / 99.9 / 99.5).

cards.cue: 'Protect S3 objects from accidental deletion and overwrite by application bugs.'
cards.answer: Enable S3 Versioning (optionally MFA Delete)
cards.why: Deletes become delete markers and overwrites keep prior versions. Object Lock is for regulatory WORM; replication does not prevent deletes.

cards.cue: 'Order processing must not lose work when a consumer crashes mid-message; failed messages after 3 attempts must be isolated for analysis.'
cards.answer: SQS queue with visibility timeout covering processing time and a dead-letter queue with maxReceiveCount 3
cards.why: Unacknowledged messages reappear after the visibility timeout; the redrive policy moves repeated failures to the DLQ. SNS has no retention; Kinesis needs consumer checkpointing.

cards.cue: SQS: max message size, max retention, max visibility timeout, max long-poll wait?
cards.answer: 256 KB / 14 days / 12 hours / 20 seconds
cards.why: Defaults are 4 days retention and 30 s visibility. Larger payloads use the Extended Client Library with S3 (up to 2 GB).

cards.cue: 'One order event must reach the billing queue, the shipping queue and the analytics Lambda, each processing independently and durably.'
cards.answer: SNS topic fan-out to multiple SQS queues (and a Lambda subscription)
cards.why: SNS pushes to many subscribers; each SQS queue gives its consumer durable, independent retry. A single SQS queue delivers each message to one consumer only.
distractors: Single SQS queue with three consumers

cards.cue: Kinesis Data Streams vs Firehose: which retains data (24 h default, up to 365 days) so multiple consumers can replay?
cards.answer: Kinesis Data Streams
cards.why: Streams is a durable, ordered log with per-shard replay. Firehose buffers 60-900 s and delivers to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch/Splunk with no storage or replay.

cards.cue: 'Existing on-prem app uses JMS/AMQP with ActiveMQ; migrate to AWS with minimal code change and Multi-AZ failover.'
cards.answer: Amazon MQ (active/standby broker)
cards.why: Amazon MQ speaks the open protocols the app already uses. SQS/SNS would require rewriting the messaging layer.

cards.cue: Step Functions Standard vs Express: max duration and delivery semantics?
cards.answer: Standard: 1 year, exactly-once; Express: 5 minutes, at-least-once (high volume)
cards.why: Standard suits long-running auditable workflows priced per transition; Express suits high-rate short event processing priced per request and duration.

cards.cue: 'ElastiCache layer must survive a node failure without cache loss and support automatic failover.' Redis or Memcached?
cards.answer: ElastiCache for Redis with Multi-AZ and automatic failover
cards.why: Redis supports replication, Multi-AZ failover and persistence. Memcached has no replication or failover - a node loss loses its data.
distractors: ElastiCache for Memcached with multiple nodes

cards.cue: 'Single EC2 instance app cannot be load balanced; users must reconnect within seconds if the instance fails.'
cards.answer: Elastic IP remapped to a standby instance (ASG min/max 1 with a script or Route 53 failover)
cards.why: An Elastic IP moves between instances in seconds and keeps the public address stable. Public IPs change on stop/start; NLB adds cost for a single target.
distractors: Rely on the auto-assigned public IP

cards.cue: 'Snapshot-restored EBS volume shows high latency on first reads; the DR runbook requires full performance immediately.'
cards.answer: Enable Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR) on the snapshot in the target AZ
cards.why: Volumes from snapshots lazily load blocks from S3; FSR pre-initializes them. Increasing IOPS does not remove first-read penalty.
distractors: Copy the snapshot to another Region

cards.cue: 'Application needs to keep working during an entire AWS Region outage with zero RPO and near-zero RTO, cost is secondary.'
cards.answer: Multi-site active/active: full stacks in two Regions, Route 53 latency/weighted routing with health checks, DynamoDB global tables / Aurora Global
cards.why: Only active/active meets near-zero RTO and RPO. Warm standby still requires scale-out and failover time.
distractors: Backup and restore with hourly snapshots

cards.cue: Lambda async invocation failure handling: how many retries and where can failures land?
cards.answer: 2 retries (3 attempts total), then a dead-letter queue (SQS/SNS) or an on-failure destination
cards.why: Sync invocations do not retry (the caller must). Event source mappings (SQS/Kinesis) have their own retry semantics and partial batch responses.

cards.cue: 'Hadoop cluster of 200 instances must minimize correlated hardware failures while allowing rack-aware placement.' Which placement group?
cards.answer: Partition placement group (up to 7 partitions per AZ)
cards.why: Partition groups isolate racks per partition and expose topology to HDFS/Cassandra/Kafka. Spread caps at 7 instances per AZ; cluster packs everything together.

cards.cue: 'On-prem file server holds 20 TB; the entire dataset must remain on-prem for low latency, with asynchronous backups to AWS for DR.' Which Storage Gateway mode?
cards.answer: Volume Gateway - stored volumes
cards.why: Stored volumes keep primary data local and ship EBS snapshots to S3. Cached volumes keep primary data in S3 with only hot data local.

cards.cue: 'Shared POSIX file system for 200 Linux EC2 instances across 3 AZs, thousands of concurrent connections.'
cards.answer: Amazon EFS (Regional)
cards.why: POSIX + multi-AZ shared access is EFS's niche; EBS is single-instance/single-AZ (Multi-Attach limited to io1/io2 same AZ); FSx for Windows is SMB.

cards.cue: 'Windows application servers need a shared file system with NTFS permissions integrated with Active Directory.'
cards.answer: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
cards.why: FSx for Windows provides SMB, NTFS ACLs, AD integration and DFS. EFS is NFS/Linux only.

cards.cue: 'Genomics HPC cluster needs hundreds of GB/s throughput and sub-millisecond latency over a dataset stored in S3, then writes results back to S3.'
cards.answer: Amazon FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket
cards.why: Lustre lazy-loads S3 objects, exports results back and delivers HPC-class throughput. EFS Max I/O is orders of magnitude slower; EBS is per instance.
distractors: EBS io2 Block Express on each node

cards.cue: 'Migrate an on-prem NetApp array; clients need NFS, SMB and iSCSI on the same data with SnapMirror replication and deduplication.'
cards.answer: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP
cards.why: ONTAP is the only multi-protocol FSx with SnapMirror, snapshots, dedup/compression. OpenZFS is NFS only; FSx for Windows is SMB only.
distractors: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server

cards.cue: 'Lift a ZFS-based Linux NFS file server to AWS keeping snapshots and instant clones; needs up to 1 million IOPS.'
cards.answer: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS
cards.why: OpenZFS provides NFS with ZFS snapshots/clones and very high IOPS. EFS lacks ZFS features and that IOPS ceiling.

cards.cue: gp3 baseline IOPS/throughput free with any size, and its maximum?
cards.answer: 3,000 IOPS + 125 MB/s baseline; up to 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MB/s provisioned independently of size
cards.why: gp2 tied IOPS to size (3 per GiB, burst 3,000). gp3 is ~20% cheaper and decouples performance from capacity.

cards.cue: 'SAP HANA database on EC2 needs 200,000 IOPS with sub-millisecond latency on a single volume.'
cards.answer: EBS io2 Block Express (up to 256,000 IOPS, 4,000 MB/s, 64 TiB)
cards.why: Only io2 Block Express exceeds 64,000 IOPS on one volume. gp3 caps at 16,000; instance store is ephemeral.

cards.cue: st1 vs sc1: max throughput of each, and can they be boot volumes?
cards.answer: st1 500 MB/s, sc1 250 MB/s; neither can boot
cards.why: Both are HDD for large sequential workloads (logs, big data, cold data). Boot requires SSD or magnetic.
distractors: st1 1,000 MB/s, sc1 500 MB/s; both boot
st1 250 MB/s, sc1 125 MB/s; st1 boots
st1 500 MB/s, sc1 250 MB/s; both boot

cards.cue: EBS Multi-Attach: which volume types and how many instances?
cards.answer: io1/io2 only, up to 16 Nitro instances in the same AZ (cluster-aware file system required)
cards.why: Multi-Attach is not a shared file system substitute; the application must coordinate writes. gp3 cannot Multi-Attach.
distractors: gp3 and io2, up to 8 instances across AZs
Any SSD type, up to 16 instances

cards.cue: 'Distributed cache node needs the highest possible local IOPS; data loss on instance stop is acceptable.'
cards.answer: EC2 instance store (NVMe) on a storage-optimized (I-family) instance
cards.why: Instance store is physically attached with millions of IOPS and no extra cost, but ephemeral. EBS adds network hops.

cards.cue: S3 request rate per prefix per second, and max object size / single PUT / multipart threshold?
cards.answer: 3,500 PUT-POST-COPY-DELETE and 5,500 GET-HEAD per prefix; 5 TB object, 5 GB single PUT, multipart recommended above 100 MB
cards.why: Prefixes are unlimited, so spreading keys across prefixes scales linearly. Multipart is mandatory above 5 GB.

cards.cue: 'Users in Asia upload multi-GB files to a bucket in us-east-1; uploads are slow.' Tempting: CloudFront.
cards.answer: S3 Transfer Acceleration (plus multipart upload)
cards.why: Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through the nearest edge onto the AWS backbone and only charges when faster. CloudFront caches downloads; it is not an upload accelerator for S3 PUTs at this scale.
distractors: CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket

cards.cue: 'Application downloads 1 GB CSVs from S3 just to read a few columns.' Cheapest way to cut transfer and latency?
cards.answer: S3 Select (SQL filtering server-side); Glacier Select for archives
cards.why: S3 Select returns only the matching subset - up to 400% faster and 80% cheaper. Athena is for ad hoc analytics across many objects.

cards.cue: 'Analysts run occasional ad hoc SQL over 50 TB of JSON logs in S3; no servers to manage; pay only when querying.'
cards.answer: Amazon Athena (with Glue Data Catalog; partition and convert to Parquet to cut $/TB scanned)
cards.why: Athena is serverless per-TB-scanned SQL on S3. Redshift needs a cluster; EMR needs cluster management.
distractors: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL loaded from S3

cards.cue: 'Discover schemas of files landing in S3, catalog them, and transform CSV to Parquet nightly with no cluster to manage.'
cards.answer: AWS Glue (crawlers + Data Catalog + ETL jobs)
cards.why: Glue is serverless Spark ETL with crawlers. EMR requires cluster management; Data Pipeline is legacy; Lambda struggles at scale.

cards.cue: 'Data science team requires a specific Spark version with custom libraries and wants Spot pricing for compute nodes.'
cards.answer: Amazon EMR with Spot task nodes
cards.why: EMR gives cluster-level control of the Hadoop ecosystem; task nodes tolerate Spot interruption. Glue abstracts the cluster away.

cards.cue: Redshift vs Redshift Spectrum vs Athena: which lets an existing Redshift cluster query S3 data in place and join with warehouse tables?
cards.answer: Redshift Spectrum
cards.why: Spectrum extends a cluster to S3 without loading. Athena is standalone serverless; Redshift alone requires COPY into managed storage.

cards.cue: 'Petabyte-scale BI with complex joins; storage and compute must scale independently.' Which Redshift option?
cards.answer: Redshift RA3 nodes with managed storage (or Redshift Serverless for intermittent use)
cards.why: RA3 separates compute from managed S3-backed storage. DC2 couples local SSD to compute; Athena is not a warehouse.

cards.cue: 'Executives need interactive dashboards over Athena and Redshift with pay-per-session pricing and embedded analytics.'
cards.answer: Amazon QuickSight (SPICE)
cards.why: QuickSight is the managed BI layer. OpenSearch Dashboards are for log analytics; Grafana is metrics-oriented.

cards.cue: 'Multiple teams query one data lake; finance must see only specific columns and rows across Athena, Redshift Spectrum and EMR.'
cards.answer: AWS Lake Formation fine-grained permissions
cards.why: Lake Formation centralizes column/row/cell-level grants across the engines. IAM and bucket policies stop at object level.

cards.cue: 'Full-text search with fuzzy matching over product catalog plus near-real-time log analytics dashboards.'
cards.answer: Amazon OpenSearch Service
cards.why: OpenSearch is the search/analytics engine with Dashboards. DynamoDB has no full-text; Athena is batch SQL.

cards.cue: 'Compute 1-minute windowed aggregations over a Kinesis stream with SQL or Flink and detect anomalies in real time.'
cards.answer: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink (formerly Kinesis Data Analytics)
cards.why: Flink is the real-time stream processor. Firehose only delivers; Athena is batch; Glue Streaming is ETL-oriented.

cards.cue: Kinesis Data Streams per-shard limits?
cards.answer: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s write; 2 MB/s read (2 MB/s per consumer with enhanced fan-out); 1 MB max record
cards.why: Shard count = peak ingest / 1 MB/s. Enhanced fan-out removes the shared 2 MB/s read ceiling across consumers.

cards.cue: 'Land clickstream data into S3 as Parquet within about a minute with zero servers and optional Lambda transformation.'
cards.answer: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
cards.why: Firehose buffers (60-900 s / 1-128 MB), converts to Parquet/ORC and delivers. Data Streams requires you to run consumers.
distractors: Kinesis Data Streams + KCL app on EC2

cards.cue: 'Existing Kafka producers and consumers must move to AWS unchanged.'
cards.answer: Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka)
cards.why: MSK is protocol-compatible Kafka. Kinesis would require rewriting clients; Amazon MQ is ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ.

cards.cue: 'Strict ordering required for 5,000 messages per second.' Tempting: SQS FIFO.
cards.answer: Kinesis Data Streams (ordering per shard) - SQS FIFO caps at 300 msg/s per action (3,000 batched) unless using many message groups with high-throughput mode
cards.why: FIFO throughput is the constraint; Kinesis scales ordered throughput by adding shards.

cards.cue: DynamoDB: max item size, and what 1 RCU / 1 WCU buys?
cards.answer: 400 KB; 1 RCU = one strongly consistent 4 KB read per second (two eventually consistent); 1 WCU = one 1 KB write per second
cards.why: Size math drives capacity planning: a 10 KB strongly consistent read costs 3 RCUs; transactional ops cost double.
distractors: 1 MB; 1 RCU = 1 KB read; 1 WCU = 4 KB write
400 KB; 1 RCU = 8 KB read; 1 WCU = 1 KB write

cards.cue: 'DynamoDB read latency must drop to microseconds for a read-heavy gaming leaderboard with minimal code change.'
cards.answer: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
cards.why: DAX is an API-compatible write-through cache for DynamoDB. ElastiCache requires application changes and is not DynamoDB-aware.

cards.cue: 'DynamoDB table throttles even though consumed capacity is well below provisioned.' Tempting: add RCUs/WCUs.
cards.answer: Hot partition - redesign the partition key for high cardinality (or write sharding); capacity is per partition (3,000 RCU / 1,000 WCU)
cards.why: Throughput is split across partitions; a hot key saturates one partition. Extra table capacity does not help a single hot key.

cards.cue: 'Delete session records automatically 24 hours after creation at no extra write cost', and 'invoke Lambda on every item change'?
cards.answer: DynamoDB TTL; DynamoDB Streams (24 h retention) with Lambda trigger
cards.why: TTL deletes expire items in the background without consuming WCUs; Streams provide an ordered change log for 24 hours.

cards.cue: Redis vs Memcached: which supports sorted sets (leaderboards), pub/sub, persistence and geospatial queries?
cards.answer: ElastiCache for Redis
cards.why: Memcached is a simple multi-threaded key-value cache with no complex data types, persistence or replication.

cards.cue: 'Redis-compatible store that must be the durable primary database (no data loss on node failure), microsecond reads.'
cards.answer: Amazon MemoryDB for Redis
cards.why: MemoryDB persists writes to a Multi-AZ transaction log. ElastiCache Redis is a cache with best-effort durability.

cards.cue: Match: 'friend-of-friend recommendations and fraud rings' / 'MongoDB API' / 'Cassandra CQL' / 'IoT sensor time series'
cards.answer: Neptune / DocumentDB / Keyspaces / Timestream
cards.why: Each is a purpose-built engine: graph, document, wide-column, time-series. Forcing these into RDS or DynamoDB is the distractor pattern.

cards.cue: 'Immutable, cryptographically verifiable history of every change to vehicle registrations, owned by one authority' vs 'multiple companies share a ledger without a central owner'?
cards.answer: Amazon QLDB for the centralized ledger; Amazon Managed Blockchain for the decentralized one
cards.why: QLDB is a single-owner journal with verifiable hashes; Managed Blockchain runs Hyperledger Fabric/Ethereum across parties.

cards.cue: 'Hundreds of Lambda functions open and drop RDS connections, exhausting max_connections.'
cards.answer: Amazon RDS Proxy
cards.why: RDS Proxy pools and shares connections, supports IAM auth, and speeds failover. Bigger instances just delay the problem.

cards.cue: 'Relational database for a dev/test app used a few hours a day with unpredictable spikes; minimize cost and admin.'
cards.answer: Aurora Serverless v2
cards.why: Serverless v2 scales ACUs in 0.5 steps and charges per second of use. Provisioned RDS bills 24x7; stopping RDS is manual and limited to 7 days.

cards.cue: Lambda limits: max timeout, max memory, max /tmp, sync payload, default Regional concurrency?
cards.answer: 15 minutes; 10 GB; 10 GB; 6 MB (256 KB async); 1,000
cards.why: Anything longer or bigger goes to Fargate, Batch or Step Functions chunking. Concurrency is a soft limit that can be raised.

cards.cue: 'Latency-sensitive API on Lambda suffers cold starts during morning ramp-up.'
cards.answer: Provisioned concurrency (optionally scheduled via Application Auto Scaling; SnapStart for Java)
cards.why: Provisioned concurrency keeps initialized environments warm. Reserved concurrency only caps/guarantees a share; more memory shortens but does not remove cold starts.
distractors: Move the function into a VPC

cards.cue: API Gateway REST API defaults: integration timeout, max payload, account throttle?
cards.answer: 29 seconds; 10 MB; 10,000 requests/s with 5,000 burst
cards.why: Long backends must go async (SQS/Step Functions) or use WebSockets. HTTP APIs share the 29 s ceiling.

cards.cue: REST API vs HTTP API vs WebSocket API: which is ~70% cheaper with lower latency but lacks API keys/usage plans, caching, WAF and request validation?
cards.answer: API Gateway HTTP API
cards.why: HTTP API is the lean proxy with JWT authorizers. REST API carries the full feature set; WebSocket is for two-way real-time.

cards.cue: 'Mobile app needs a single GraphQL endpoint aggregating DynamoDB and Lambda with real-time subscriptions and offline sync.'
cards.answer: AWS AppSync
cards.why: AppSync is managed GraphQL with subscriptions over WebSockets. API Gateway WebSocket API needs custom routing logic; REST has no subscriptions.

cards.cue: 'Run containers with no cluster or host management; pay per vCPU-second' vs 'must use existing Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts'?
cards.answer: AWS Fargate (ECS) for the first; Amazon EKS for the second (EKS can also run on Fargate)
cards.why: Fargate removes host management; EKS provides Kubernetes API compatibility. ECS on EC2 means you patch and scale hosts.

cards.cue: 'Nightly job renders 4,000 videos, each taking 40 minutes; must be cheap and retry failures.' Tempting: Lambda.
cards.answer: AWS Batch (or ECS/Fargate tasks) with Spot capacity - Lambda's 15-minute limit rules it out
cards.why: Batch manages job queues, retries and Spot. Step Functions could orchestrate but still needs a long-running compute target.

cards.cue: 'Deploy a Java web app quickly with managed capacity provisioning, load balancing and health monitoring while retaining access to the underlying EC2 instances' vs 'simplest possible deployment of a container from source with no infrastructure visibility'?
cards.answer: AWS Elastic Beanstalk; AWS App Runner
cards.why: Beanstalk is PaaS with EC2 control; App Runner is fully abstracted for web apps/APIs from source or image.

cards.cue: 'Tightly coupled MPI weather simulation needs the lowest inter-node latency and highest bandwidth.'
cards.answer: Cluster placement group with EFA-enabled instances in one AZ
cards.why: Cluster groups pack instances on the same rack segment; EFA provides OS-bypass networking. Spread/partition trade latency for fault isolation.
distractors: Auto Scaling group across AZs with ENA

cards.cue: Spread placement group max instances per AZ, and partition placement group max partitions per AZ?
cards.answer: 7 and 7
cards.why: Spread limits reflect distinct racks per AZ; partition groups can hold hundreds of instances across up to 7 partitions per AZ.

cards.cue: 'Global multiplayer game over UDP needs static IPs that never change and fast failover between Regions.' Tempting: CloudFront.
cards.answer: AWS Global Accelerator (2 static anycast IPs, TCP/UDP, no caching)
cards.why: CloudFront is an HTTP cache; it cannot proxy UDP or provide static IPs. Global Accelerator routes L4 over the backbone with health-based failover.

cards.cue: 'Serve a static website and images globally with HTTPS, lowest latency and lowest cost.'
cards.answer: S3 static hosting + CloudFront with ACM certificate (OAC to lock the bucket)
cards.why: CloudFront caches at the edge and terminates TLS (S3 websites do not support HTTPS directly). EC2 or Global Accelerator add cost without caching benefits.
distractors: EC2 web servers behind an ALB in three Regions
Global Accelerator in front of S3

cards.cue: CloudFront Functions vs Lambda@Edge: which one for sub-millisecond header rewrites on viewer requests at millions of requests per second, and its memory/time limits?
cards.answer: CloudFront Functions - 2 MB memory, <1 ms, viewer request/response only, JavaScript
cards.why: Lambda@Edge handles origin events, network calls and bodies with 5 s viewer / 30 s origin limits, at ~6x the price.
distractors: CloudFront Functions - 128 MB, 30 s, all four events

cards.cue: 'Paying subscribers must access an entire HLS video library (thousands of segment files) via CloudFront without altering URLs.'
cards.answer: CloudFront signed cookies
cards.why: Signed cookies authorize many objects at once; signed URLs are per object. Field-level encryption protects POST data, not access.

cards.cue: Route 53: 'users in Germany must be served only from the Frankfurt stack for data-residency law' vs 'send users to whichever Region responds fastest'?
cards.answer: Geolocation routing; Latency routing
cards.why: Geolocation keys on the user's location (compliance); latency keys on measured performance. Geoproximity adjusts by distance bias.

cards.cue: Route 53 multivalue answer: max healthy records returned, and is it a load balancer replacement?
cards.answer: Up to 8 healthy records; no - it is DNS-level client-side distribution with health checks
cards.why: Multivalue improves availability cheaply but lacks connection draining, L7 routing and instant failover of an ELB.
distractors: Up to 8; yes it replaces ALB

cards.cue: 'Company now has 60 VPCs across 5 accounts plus a data center; full-mesh peering is unmanageable.'
cards.answer: AWS Transit Gateway (share via RAM; up to 5,000 attachments; transitive routing)
cards.why: TGW is the hub with route tables for segmentation; peering is 1:1 and non-transitive. PrivateLink is for exposing single services.

cards.cue: 'Two VPCs in different accounts and Regions with non-overlapping CIDRs need private connectivity; lowest cost, no transitive requirement.'
cards.answer: VPC peering (inter-Region)
cards.why: Peering is free for same-AZ traffic and has no hourly fee; TGW charges per attachment and per GB.

cards.cue: Direct Connect dedicated speeds, Site-to-Site VPN per-tunnel throughput, and TGW max attachments?
cards.answer: 1 / 10 / 100 Gbps (hosted 50 Mbps-10 Gbps); 1.25 Gbps per tunnel (2 tunnels); 5,000 attachments
cards.why: VPN over TGW with ECMP aggregates tunnels; DX takes weeks to months to provision so VPN is the quick or backup path.

cards.cue: 'Connect the data center to AWS today with encryption; a 10 Gbps private link will arrive in 3 months.' Interim and final design?
cards.answer: Site-to-Site VPN now (minutes to deploy), then Direct Connect with the VPN kept as encrypted backup
cards.why: VPN is fast to provision over the internet; DX offers consistent bandwidth later. Client VPN is for individual users, not sites.
distractors: AWS Client VPN for the data center

cards.cue: 'Remote employees on laptops need secure access to private VPC resources with corporate SAML authentication.'
cards.answer: AWS Client VPN
cards.why: Client VPN is the managed OpenVPN endpoint with AD/SAML/certificate auth. Site-to-Site VPN connects networks, not users.

cards.cue: CloudWatch: EC2 standard vs detailed monitoring interval, and minimum resolution for custom metrics? Also how to get memory and disk metrics?
cards.answer: 5 minutes standard / 1 minute detailed; 1 second high-resolution custom metrics; install the CloudWatch agent for memory/disk
cards.why: Hypervisor metrics exclude OS-level memory/disk. Detailed monitoring costs extra but enables faster scaling reactions.
distractors: 1 min / 10 s; 1 min; enable detailed monitoring
5 min / 1 min; 1 min; use EC2 status checks

cards.cue: 'Find which microservice adds latency in a request that traverses API Gateway, Lambda and DynamoDB.'
cards.answer: AWS X-Ray tracing
cards.why: X-Ray produces end-to-end traces and a service map. CloudWatch Logs show per-service logs; CloudTrail is API audit.

cards.cue: 'Single-digit millisecond latency for users in a metro area far from any Region' vs '5G mobile edge' vs 'AWS services on-prem for data residency'?
cards.answer: Local Zones; Wavelength; Outposts
cards.why: Each extends AWS infrastructure to a different edge: metro, carrier 5G network, customer data center.

cards.cue: 'Share one Transit Gateway and a set of subnets with other accounts in the organization without duplicating them.'
cards.answer: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM)
cards.why: RAM shares TGWs, subnets, Route 53 Resolver rules, License Manager configs across accounts. Peering or copying resources is the distractor.

cards.cue: 'Logs are written once, must be kept 7 years, rarely read, and a 12-hour retrieval delay is acceptable.' Cheapest class?
cards.answer: S3 Glacier Deep Archive (180-day minimum; Standard retrieval 12 h, Bulk 48 h)
cards.why: Deep Archive is the cheapest per GB. Glacier Flexible costs ~4x more per GB for a faster restore that was not required.

cards.cue: Glacier Flexible Retrieval tiers and times; Deep Archive tiers and times?
cards.answer: Expedited 1-5 min / Standard 3-5 h / Bulk 5-12 h; Deep Archive Standard 12 h / Bulk 48 h
cards.why: Bulk is the cheapest (free for Flexible); Expedited is not available for Deep Archive. Glacier Instant Retrieval is milliseconds.
distractors: Expedited 1 h / Standard 12 h / Bulk 48 h; Deep 3-5 h
Expedited 1-5 min / Standard 1 h / Bulk 3 h; Deep 12 h
All Glacier classes 3-5 h; Deep 24 h

cards.cue: S3 minimum storage durations: Standard-IA / One Zone-IA / Glacier Instant / Glacier Flexible / Deep Archive, and the IA minimum billable object size?
cards.why: Deleting or transitioning earlier bills the remainder. Objects under 128 KB in IA are billed as 128 KB; Intelligent-Tiering does not tier them.

cards.cue: Spot the trap: 'Application logs are kept 7 days then deleted; to save money, transition them to Standard-IA after 1 day.'
cards.answer: Wrong - IA has a 30-day minimum charge and lifecycle cannot move objects to IA before 30 days; keep Standard with a 7-day expiration rule
cards.why: Short-lived data never benefits from IA/Glacier minimums. Expiration is the only cost lever here.

cards.cue: 'Access patterns for 500 TB of media are unknown and change over time; minimize cost without retrieval fees.'
cards.answer: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
cards.why: IT moves objects between tiers automatically for a small monitoring fee and no retrieval charge. Choosing IA blindly risks retrieval fees on hot objects.
distractors: S3 Standard with lifecycle to Glacier after 30 days

cards.cue: 'Thumbnails regenerated from originals on demand; accessed rarely; cheapest with millisecond access.' vs 'monthly financial backups that must survive an AZ loss'?
cards.answer: S3 One Zone-IA for thumbnails; S3 Standard-IA for the backups
cards.why: One Zone-IA is ~20% cheaper but single-AZ, so only for re-creatable data. Standard-IA is multi-AZ.

cards.cue: 'Medical images accessed about once per quarter but must open instantly when requested.' Tempting: Glacier Flexible.
cards.answer: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (milliseconds, 90-day minimum)
cards.why: Flexible takes minutes to hours. Instant Retrieval is cheaper than Standard-IA for quarterly access while keeping ms latency.

cards.cue: Purchasing discount ceilings: Spot / Standard RI and EC2 Instance SP / Convertible RI and Compute SP? And Spot's interruption notice?
cards.answer: Up to 90% / 72% / 66%; 2-minute warning
cards.why: Discount tracks flexibility inversely: more flexibility, less discount. Spot pays for tolerating interruption.

cards.cue: 'Steady baseline compute for 3 years; the team will move between instance families, Regions and to Fargate over time; lowest cost with least management.'
cards.answer: Compute Savings Plan (1 or 3 year, $/hour commitment)
cards.why: Compute SPs apply across family/Region/OS/tenancy and cover Fargate and Lambda. Standard RIs lock family; Convertible RIs need manual exchanges.

cards.cue: 'Must use Reserved Instances (policy), but the instance family may change during the 3-year term.'
cards.answer: Convertible Reserved Instances (up to 66%, exchangeable)
cards.why: Standard RIs only flex size within a family. Convertible RIs can be exchanged for different family/OS/tenancy of equal or greater value.

cards.cue: 'Guarantee 50 c5.xlarge in us-east-1a for a two-week event, no long commitment, cheapest.'
cards.answer: On-Demand Capacity Reservation (stack with an existing Savings Plan/regional RI for discount)
cards.why: Capacity Reservations hold AZ capacity for any duration at On-Demand price. Zonal RIs need a 1-year term; Spot cannot guarantee capacity.

cards.cue: 'Bring existing per-socket Windows Server and SQL Server licenses to AWS.' Dedicated Host or Dedicated Instance?
cards.answer: Dedicated Hosts (visibility into sockets and cores, host affinity; track with License Manager)
cards.why: Dedicated Instances give hardware isolation but no socket/core visibility, so socket-bound licenses cannot be applied.

cards.cue: 'Image-processing queue tolerates interruption and reprocessing; cut EC2 cost by up to 90%.'
cards.answer: EC2 Spot Instances via Spot Fleet or ASG mixed instances policy with capacity rebalancing
cards.why: Stateless, retryable work is the Spot sweet spot; diversify instance types to reduce interruption. RIs save less and commit long term.
distractors: Compute Savings Plan on the whole fleet

cards.cue: 'Traffic doubles every weekday at 9:00 and instances take 8 minutes to boot' vs 'keep average CPU near 50%' vs 'add 2 instances at 70% CPU and 4 at 85%'?
cards.answer: Scheduled (or predictive) scaling; target tracking; step scaling
cards.why: Predictable time-based load needs pre-warming; steady proportional control is target tracking; graded alarm responses are step scaling.

cards.cue: Predictive scaling: minimum and ideal history, and Compute Optimizer default lookback?
cards.answer: At least 24 hours, ideally 14 days; 14 days (up to 93 with enhanced infrastructure metrics)
cards.why: Both learn from CloudWatch history; short histories produce weak recommendations.

cards.cue: 'Identify over-provisioned EC2, EBS volumes and Lambda memory across the organization with specific recommended sizes.'
cards.answer: AWS Compute Optimizer
cards.why: Compute Optimizer gives ML-based right-sizing recommendations. Trusted Advisor flags low utilization broadly; Cost Explorer rightsizing covers EC2 only.

cards.cue: Cost Explorer vs Budgets vs Cost and Usage Report: which one alerts when forecasted spend exceeds 80% and can stop instances?
cards.answer: AWS Budgets (with Budget Actions)
cards.why: Cost Explorer visualizes/forecasts (13 months back, 12 forward); CUR is raw hourly line items to S3 for Athena/QuickSight.

cards.cue: 'Finance wants hourly resource-level billing data joined with tags in their own BI tool.'
cards.answer: AWS Cost and Usage Report delivered to S3, queried with Athena/QuickSight
cards.why: CUR is the most granular dataset. Cost Explorer is a UI/API with limited granularity; Budgets is alerts.

cards.cue: Cost Explorer history and forecast horizon; CloudTrail event history retention without a trail?
cards.answer: 13 months back / 12 months forecast; 90 days
cards.why: Longer analysis needs CUR; longer audit needs a trail to S3.

cards.cue: 'Automated checks for idle load balancers, underutilized EBS, service-quota usage and open security groups; company has Business Support.'
cards.answer: AWS Trusted Advisor (full checks with Business/Enterprise support)
cards.why: Trusted Advisor spans cost, performance, security, fault tolerance, quotas and operational excellence. Basic support only gets core checks.

cards.cue: Data transfer per GB: internet egress / inter-Region / inter-AZ / same-AZ via private IP?
cards.answer: ~$0.09 (first 100 GB/month free) / ~$0.02 / $0.01 each direction / free
cards.why: Inbound is always free. Traffic over public or Elastic IPs inside a Region is billed as Regional transfer even in the same AZ.

cards.cue: Spot the trap: 'Two EC2 instances in the same AZ exchange 50 TB/month and incur transfer charges; fix by moving them to one subnet.'
cards.answer: Wrong - the charge comes from using public/Elastic IPs; switch to private IP addresses (same subnet is irrelevant)
cards.why: Same-AZ transfer is free only over private IPs. Cross-AZ costs $0.01/GB each direction regardless of subnet.
distractors: Correct - same subnet makes it free

cards.cue: 'NAT gateway bill exploded after private instances started pushing 100 TB/month to S3.'
cards.answer: Add an S3 gateway endpoint so S3 traffic bypasses the NAT gateway (free; NAT charges $0.045/GB processed)
cards.why: Gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB are free and remove NAT data-processing fees. Interface endpoints ($0.01/GB) fit other services.
distractors: Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance

cards.cue: 'Serve 200 TB/month of downloads from S3 to global users; reduce egress cost.'
cards.answer: Put CloudFront in front of S3 (S3 -> CloudFront transfer is free; CloudFront egress is cheaper than S3 egress)
cards.why: CloudFront also caches, reducing S3 GET requests. Transfer Acceleration is for uploads; Global Accelerator does not cache.

cards.cue: 'Migrate 100 TB over a 1 Gbps link that production already uses heavily; deadline 10 days.' Tempting: DataSync.
cards.answer: AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized (80 TB usable each) - 1 Gbps moves ~10 TB/day at best, so 100 TB needs 10+ days of a saturated link
cards.why: Rule: 1 Gbps ~ 10 TB/day. Anything over a week or on a contended link goes offline. Snowmobile is only for >10 PB.
distractors: AWS DataSync over the existing link

cards.cue: Snowball Edge Storage Optimized usable capacity / Snowcone / Snowmobile? And DataSync max per agent?
cards.answer: 80 TB (210 TB variant) / 8 TB HDD or 14 TB SSD / 100 PB; 10 Gbps per agent
cards.why: Snow devices import into S3 Standard first (lifecycle to Glacier afterward). Snowcone can also run a DataSync agent for online transfer.

cards.cue: 'Move 30 TB from an on-prem NFS share to Amazon EFS over an existing 10 Gbps Direct Connect, with incremental weekly syncs and integrity verification.'
cards.answer: AWS DataSync (agent on-prem)
cards.why: DataSync is purpose-built for online NFS/SMB migration with scheduling and verification. Snowball is offline; Storage Gateway is for ongoing access, not migration.

cards.cue: 'Partners deliver files via SFTP; replace the self-managed SFTP server on EC2 and land files in S3.'
cards.answer: AWS Transfer Family (SFTP endpoint to S3)
cards.why: Transfer Family is the managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2 service with custom identity providers. DataSync needs an agent, not an SFTP protocol endpoint.

cards.cue: 'On-prem applications write files over NFS/SMB; files must become S3 objects with lifecycle to Glacier while a local cache keeps recent files fast.'
cards.answer: Storage Gateway - S3 File Gateway
cards.why: File Gateway maps files to native S3 objects with a local cache. Volume Gateway presents iSCSI blocks; Tape Gateway needs backup software.

cards.cue: Volume Gateway cached vs stored: max volume size of each, and which keeps primary data in S3?
cards.answer: Cached 32 TiB (primary in S3, hot subset local); stored 16 TiB (primary on-prem, async snapshots to AWS)
cards.why: Cached lets you expand on-prem storage into S3; stored is for low-latency full local datasets with cloud backup.
distractors: Cached 16 TiB; stored 32 TiB; stored keeps primary in S3
Both 64 TiB; cached keeps primary on-prem
Cached 1 PiB; stored 16 TiB; both primary in S3

cards.cue: 'Eliminate the physical tape library while keeping NetBackup unchanged; archive tapes to the cheapest storage.'
cards.answer: Storage Gateway - Tape Gateway (virtual tapes in S3, archived to Glacier Flexible / Deep Archive)
cards.why: Tape Gateway presents an iSCSI VTL the backup software already understands. File Gateway would require changing the backup workflow.

cards.cue: 'Migrate an on-prem Oracle database to Aurora PostgreSQL with near-zero downtime; source stays live during migration.'
cards.answer: AWS DMS with continuous replication (CDC) plus Schema Conversion Tool for the schema
cards.why: DMS handles heterogeneous migrations with ongoing change capture; SCT converts Oracle schema/code. Snapshot restore does not cross engines.

cards.cue: 'Rehost 200 VMware VMs to EC2 with continuous replication and a short cutover window.'
cards.answer: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN)
cards.why: MGN replicates servers at block level and launches EC2 test/cutover instances. DMS is databases; DataSync is files.

cards.cue: 'Reduce RDS cost for a production database that must remain highly available' vs 'dev database used only during office hours'?
cards.answer: Reserved Instances for the production Multi-AZ instance; stop the dev instance outside hours (auto-restarts after 7 days) or use Aurora Serverless v2
cards.why: Multi-AZ cannot be removed from prod without losing HA, so commit pricing is the lever; dev load is intermittent so stop or scale to zero.
distractors: Disable Multi-AZ on prod; Reserved Instances for dev
Convertible RI for dev; On-Demand for prod

cards.cue: 'DynamoDB table with steady predictable load' vs 'new table with unknown spiky traffic' - capacity mode for each?
cards.answer: Provisioned with auto scaling (plus reserved capacity) for steady; On-Demand for unknown/spiky
cards.why: On-Demand costs several times more per request but never throttles or over-provisions. Standard-IA table class for rarely accessed data.

cards.cue: 'Deploy the same baseline IAM roles and Config rules to 80 accounts in 3 Regions from one place' vs 'let teams self-provision pre-approved architectures'?
cards.answer: CloudFormation StackSets; AWS Service Catalog
cards.why: StackSets pushes stacks across accounts/Regions; Service Catalog curates approved products with constraints for end users.

cards.cue: 'Schedule a nightly Lambda at 02:00 and route Zendesk SaaS events to different targets by ticket priority.'
cards.answer: Amazon EventBridge (Scheduler + partner event source + content-filtering rules)
cards.why: EventBridge handles cron schedules, SaaS partner buses and content-based routing. SNS filters only on attributes and has no schedules or SaaS sources.

cards.cue: Exam mechanics: duration, question count and scoring, passing score?
cards.answer: 130 minutes; 65 questions (50 scored + 15 unscored); 720 of 1000 scaled
cards.why: Two minutes per question. Unscored items are indistinguishable, so do not panic on strange questions. No guessing penalty.

cards.cue: 'Insert a third-party next-generation firewall fleet inline for all inbound traffic, scaling transparently' vs 'HTTP path routing to containers' vs 'static IP per AZ for TCP'?
cards.answer: Gateway Load Balancer; Application Load Balancer; Network Load Balancer
cards.why: GWLB (GENEVE) is for appliances, ALB for L7, NLB for L4 with Elastic IPs. CLB is legacy.

cards.cue: 'Employees authenticate against the on-prem SAML 2.0 identity provider and must get temporary credentials for an IAM role in ONE account without IAM users.' Which STS call and integration?
cards.answer: IAM SAML 2.0 federation: IdP trust + role trust policy, STS AssumeRoleWithSAML (OIDC web identities use AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity; multi-account workforce use IAM Identity Center)
cards.why: AssumeRoleWithSAML exchanges the IdP assertion for role credentials (15 min-12 h). Cognito is for app end users; IAM users would duplicate identities.
distractors: Cognito user pool with SAML federation
IAM users synced from AD via SCIM

cards.cue: Athena pricing unit, and the three levers that cut the bill?
cards.answer: $5 per TB scanned; partition the data, convert to columnar Parquet/ORC, and compress
cards.why: Athena bills on bytes scanned (10 MB minimum per query). Columnar formats let it read only needed columns; partitions prune files; compression shrinks bytes.
distractors: $0.09 per GB returned; cache in CloudFront

cards.cue: Aurora Global Database replication lag and Spot interruption notice - two 'time' numbers the exam loves?
cards.answer: Typically < 1 second lag (RPO ~1 s, RTO < 1 min); Spot gives a 2-minute interruption warning
cards.why: Aurora Global replicates at the storage layer across Regions; Spot's 2-minute notice arrives via EventBridge/instance metadata so workloads can checkpoint.
